description: We are a team of three from Chile: two astronomers and one software engineer. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge we built SPHEREx Blink, a public web tool that shows how the infrared sky changed between SPHEREx visits: an image series like a short video, a view of what got brighter, fainter or moved, and spectra and brightness checks for any object. We combine astronomical data analysis, Python, backend development and web deployment.
summary: We built SPHEREx Blink, a public web tool that turns SPHEREx images into a short movie of any patch of sky. Anyone can type a name or RA/Dec, choose a field of view (3–20′) and one of the six detectors. They then see every DR1 and QR3 image of that spot in time order, with its date and wavelength. Moving objects stand out in the blink and in a "what changed" view that compares survey passes. Users can also stack or subtract images from different dates, overlay Gaia and WISE sources, and check each image's quality flags. Two more tools go beyond the pictures. One measures a spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm from the same images. The other tests whether a star changes in brightness compared with its neighbours. The tool reads only the pixels it needs straight from NASA's cloud archive, so it needs no copy of the data, and a new release is added in one line. We tested it on the five challenge targets. Barnard's Star visibly moves, RW Aur and R Dra vary, and Epsilon Indi B shows the spectrum of a T dwarf. WISE 0855 sits at SPHEREx's detection limit.
details:
What it does. SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool that lets anyone see how the infrared sky changed between the dates NASA's SPHEREx telescope observed it. You open a full-screen sky map, pick a star or any spot (or type a name or coordinates), choose the field of view, and the real SPHEREx images of that place play one after another like a short video. Every frame shows its date and wavelength.

From there you can:

  • stack each survey pass and compare passes;
  • open "What changed", where constant stars stay grey and only real changes are coloured: orange if a star got brighter, blue if it got fainter, both side by side if it moved;
  • add or subtract any images you choose;
  • measure the object's spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm, image by image;
  • check whether its brightness changes compared with the stars around it;
  • compare the field with other surveys (GALEX, DSS2, 2MASS, Spitzer, WISE, Herschel, Planck).

Every view lives in the page address, so it can be shared.

How it works. The backend searches the official SPHEREx releases (DR1 and the weekly QR3) at NASA/IPAC IRSA. Instead of downloading 65 MB files, it reads only the bytes it needs straight from the public cloud bucket: 4 small requests per image. It then applies the official recipe to hide flagged pixels, removes the zodiacal background, aligns every image north-up and renders the pictures. Spectra use the official per-pixel wavelength and solid-angle calibration. Nothing is stored in advance, so new data releases appear automatically.

Benefits and impact. SPHEREx data is powerful but hard to use: each pixel sees a different wavelength, and the files are large and technical. Our tool turns it into something a student, a teacher or an amateur astronomer can explore in a few clicks, and every measurement is explained in the page. For researchers it is a fast first look: is this source variable, did it move, what does its spectrum look like?

Tools. Python with FastAPI, astropy, reproject, sep, NumPy and SciPy for the backend (hosted on Render). React, TypeScript and Vite for the frontend (hosted on Vercel). Aladin Lite (CDS) for the sky map. Data from NASA/IPAC IRSA and ESA Gaia.

What makes it creative. A plain difference between two dates leaves a black-and-white mark on every star, because SPHEREx sees each star at a different wavelength and with very few pixels. We divide the change by each star's own brightness, so constant stars fade out and only what really changed stands out. The same idea, comparing each star with itself at the same wavelength, powers the brightness check. Saturated stars are followed through the wings of their image.

What we considered.

  • Scientific honesty: every result was checked against real data before showing it. RW Aur comes out variable (41 % against 3 % for constant stars); eps Ind B and Barnard's Star come out stable; Barnard's Star is seen moving north; the brown dwarf eps Ind B shows its water and methane bands.
  • Limits stated plainly: changes under about 10 % are not coloured, and saturated stars can only be followed in relative units.
  • Speed on free hosting, use on phones, and clear explanations for people without an astronomy background.
  • We also built a period search, but left it out because it was slow and the challenge only asks whether the sky changes.
